title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 (computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5)). An exploratory paired bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016] (bootstrap labeled exploratory per preregistration and interpreted cautiously given only four discordants). Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, provide execution accounting and representative validator traces, and give explicit artifact pointers and hashes for reproducibility.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern large language models (LLMs) show promise for translating human intent to device configuration, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and exploratory paired bootstrap CI descriptions with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and practical external‑validity limits.
sections.related_work: Three converging literatures inform the reliability challenge for LLM‑driven NetOps and motivate a GVR architecture. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration, while emphasizing hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers [doi:10.1145/3718958.3750537; https://openalex.org/W4411735779]. Intent‑driven configuration prototypes typically pair generators with ad‑hoc validation or operator oversight rather than large, controlled trials against deterministic verifiers [doi:10.1002/nem.2313]. Second, methodological work advocates explicit generate‑validate‑repair evaluation practices and standardized validator semantics; these papers call for paired, preregistered trials that quantify verifier coverage, failure modes, and orchestration costs [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, deterministic configuration verifiers and scalable verification systems (Batfish‑derived and localized subspecification approaches) provide concrete oracles for many syntactic and workflow properties but have known abstraction limits that affect operational sufficiency [https://openalex.org/W4413757123]. Our experiment situates itself at the intersection of these literatures by empirically measuring a bounded GVR controller against the identical shared initial candidate per intent in a preregistered paired design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory plan: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N = 500 distinct intents stratified evenly across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Sampling seeds, the deterministic task generator, and the analysis executor were frozen before execution (preregistration SHA‑256 = aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a). The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; an exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as a descriptive interval.

Generation, orchestration, and budget: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model gpt-5-mini; the recorded generation configuration is archived (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = a40e96e2...). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and invoked at most one automated repair call when the verifier returned violations (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Provider accounting from the execution manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 with stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4; total model_calls_used = 504.

Deterministic verifier semantics and repair policy: The primary verifier implements a deterministic pipeline on normalized CLI sequences: syntactic parsing, canonical normalization, required‑sequence/workflow checks (must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change patterns), availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups), dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields), and final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome; per‑episode verifier_trace objects (validation_before, validation_after, violation list, valid boolean) are archived under execution/scoring/ and indexed by the execution manifest. If verification fails, the GVR controller issues at most one repair prompt to the same model including the intent abstraction and verifier violation codes; a repair candidate is accepted only if the verifier returns valid=true for the subsequent candidate.
sections.results:
Execution and primary counts: The run completed completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions) with model_calls_used = 504. analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates; all four repair attempts produced subsequent verifier passes and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; repaired pairs used 2 model calls each (shared_initial + one repair). Exact McNemar and bootstrap: the preregistered conditional exact McNemar conditions on observed discordant margin n = 4 and yields two‑sided p = 0.125 (p = 2*(1/2)^4). The exploratory paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) gives a 95% percentile interval [0.002, 0.016]; the bootstrap is reported as exploratory per the preregistration and interpreted cautiously given the small discordant count.

Concise repaired‑pair table (artifact‑grounded): the following table lists the four repaired/discordant pairs with the verifier violation code(s) reported in the archived per‑episode traces, one‑line human‑readable descriptions, whether the controller invoked a repair, model calls used for the pair, and the final verifier outcome. All per‑pair details and violation codes are recorded in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef5cc5a237a3361f18f45fabf14cd23a1c679556f65477f9f681915d02) and in the per‑episode scorer JSON objects under execution/scoring/; auditors may retrieve exact per‑pair JSON entries from those artifacts.

- pair-000090 — violation code(s): REQ_SEQ_VIOLATION — description: required sequencing (must down → change → restore) not satisfied; repair invoked: yes; model calls for pair: 2; final score (verifier): PASS.
- pair-000341 — violation code(s): AVAILABILITY_GROUP_VIOLATION — description: availability/group constraint (exactly_active/minimum_in_group) violated; repair invoked: yes; model calls for pair: 2; final score: PASS.
- pair-000381 — violation code(s): PAIRED_FIELD_DEP_VIOLATION — description: paired‑field dependency (both MTUs must be changed atomically) violated; repair invoked: yes; model calls for pair: 2; final score: PASS.
- pair-000413 — violation code(s): MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD_VIOLATION — description: field change performed without required interface down transition; repair invoked: yes; model calls for pair: 2; final score: PASS.

(These per‑pair violation code labels and one‑line descriptions are verbatim summaries taken from the archived per‑episode verifier_trace objects in execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/scoring/*.json; see execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = fe9b93ef... and deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256 = 48bafa8c... for provider_call and stage accounting.)
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and reconciliation of inferential outcomes: The GVR pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that the baseline condition would have accepted; these repairs account for the entire observed paired difference (0.008). Under the preregistered conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but should be considered descriptive: bootstrap resampling does not condition on the observed discordant margin and percentile intervals at extremely small discordant counts have reduced frequentist coverage properties. We therefore follow the preregistered McNemar decision rule for primary inference and report the bootstrap interval as exploratory.

Verifier coverage and operational sufficiency: The deterministic verifier enforces the canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. These checks detect a broad class of syntactic and workflow errors in our synthetic intent grammar and were sufficient to flag the four repaired episodes. However, the verifier does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence, session‑level failures, or resource limits; passing the verifier is necessary for safety under the encoded rule set but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Expanding verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence modeling) is therefore essential prior to any automated production application.

Operational cost tradeoffs: The observed repair rate (4/500 = 0.8%) produced modest additional model‑call overhead (4 repair calls on top of 500 shared_initial calls). Provider accounting recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 504 with stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. In environments with low baseline verifier‑detectable failure rates, a low‑latency deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair loop can intercept verifier‑detectable hazards at modest model cost; real deployments must test adversarial inputs, diverse intent distributions, and verifier runtime on full inventories to quantify operational latency and cost tradeoffs.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at low model‑call overhead (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator (which was not executed in this run). All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; see the archived execution manifest for full artifact paths and hashes.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
